title: Multi-Agent Foundation Models for Urban Mobility: The Malmö Elderly Case
authors: Biscalchin A.; Sarkheyli E.; Sarkheyli-Hagele A.
abstract: Understanding travel behaviour is crucial for developing inclusive, adaptable transportation systems in ageing cities. Yet many public authorities lack the expertise and budget for advanced analytics. We present a modular, multi-agent framework that employs Large Language Models (LLMs) to lower the entry barrier to data-driven mobility analysis. The pipeline extracts interpretable, policy-oriented insights from unstructured survey data and outputs structured reports without manual coding. We demonstrate the approach using Malmö's 2023 travel survey for residents aged 65+, and benchmark its recommendations against those of (i) a single-agent LLM service (Single Agent), representative of current commercial offerings, and (ii) a human expert baseline (Human), both evaluated in a blinded expert review. The system achieves superior reasoning quality compared to the single-agent baseline, while performing slightly lower on interpretability and focus, and approaches expert-level quality overall - at a fraction of the cost and effort. Key constraints are the current lack of real-time data ingestion and dependence on proprietary commercial APIs. The study provides an open-source proof of concept showing how multi-agent LLMs can make urban mobility analytics more accessible, transparent, and timely. All code and evaluation materials are publicly available.

title: Zero-Shot and Few-Shot Synthetic Question-Answer Generation with a Hungarian Large Language Model on Consumer Complaint Data
authors: Szappan A.; Krutilla Z.
abstract: A comparative evaluation of large generative language models for the task of synthetic question-answer generation in Hungarian is presented in this study. The analysis is based on a Hungarian-language corpus compiled from anonymized consumer complaint letters published on the official website of the Hungarian consumer protection authority. The evaluated models were tested using zero-shot and few-shot prompting strategies under quantized inference in a resource-constrained hardware environment equipped with a GPU limited to 6 GB of VRAM. The objective of the study was to assess whether contemporary language models with several billion parameters are capable of generating formal, legally neutral responses without relying on explicit metadata or additional structural guidance. Experimental results indicate that, in a local low-resource setting with quantized model variants, the examined models do not consistently produce structurally coherent and stable outputs. Structural and contextual deficiencies were frequently observed, along with generation instabilities such as degenerative repetition. Furthermore, it is demonstrated by the experiments that generation parameters and the amount of contextual input significantly influence response quality. Beyond qualitative observations, the findings provide practical insights into the achievable performance and limitations of deploying contemporary language models in constrained hardware environments, highlighting the trade-offs between model size, inference configuration, and output reliability in low-resource deployment scenarios.

title: The Quality Assessment of LLM in Digital Forensics
authors: Costantini F.; Galvan F.; Montessoro P.L.; Crisci F.; Baron L.
abstract: The utilisation of Artificial Intelligence in investigative contexts facilitates the optimisation of the analysis of digital artefacts, which can be collected in a variety of formats, including text, printouts, images, and videos, as well as from diverse sources, such as datasets, networks, and devices. More recently, while the adoption of LLM (Large Language Models) appears to hold significant potentials, it is also accompanied by emerging concerns relating to its technological limitations, including distortions and hallucinations, which can hinder law enforcement and compromise the balance between the rights of the accused and the power of the judicial authorities. Notwithstanding the activities prohibited by Art. 5 of the AI ACT, the fact is that LLM technologies are already assuming a pivotal role in investigations, yet are still inadequate the principles, methodologies and tools allowing courts to assess accuracy and precision of the language models before implementing them. The objective of this research project is to develop a methodology that can be adopted for the assessment and comparison of LLMs in performing analytical processes. To this end, a synthetic dataset of electronic evidence is generated from a fictitious criminal scenario and fed to the agent with engineered prompting techniques.

title: Digital Revenants: Voices of the Dead in the Age of AI
authors: Ramello S.
abstract: Artificial intelligence now lets the living send the voices of the dead into public life, whether through a courtroom recording or a political campaign. A grieving family or an advocacy group rebuilds a dead speaker and assigns the words the recreated voice will carry. Debates on griefbots and digital immortality have mapped the ethical strains yet leave unexamined the mechanism by which the living lend a posthumous voice public authority. This article introduces anticipatory selection, the operation by which the living fix the wording and the scene of a reconstructed voice before any word is heard. Large language models and simpler cloning tools generate speech under conditions arranged in advance, so the dead arrive already cast in a chosen role. Because authority for the speaker gathers across many separate hands, no lone author answers for the result, and the figure named can no longer reply. The governing issue is one of jurisdiction, of the terms that settle which of the dead may speak in public. Authenticity has ceased to be the point. Because the living now hold those terms, the public that receives the return may fairly demand that whoever composed the voice account for the choice.

title: Decision gatekeepers: how hedonic vs. utilitarian products shape differential persuasion effects in LLM-mediated recommendations
authors: Pescher A.
abstract: As consumers increasingly rely on AI for purchase guidance, large language models (LLMs) have become key mediators of buying decisions, processing marketing content before generating recommendations. Understanding how these AI-based decision support systems respond to persuasive techniques becomes critical for consumers and system designers. This study maps LLM response patterns to persuasive techniques across product types. Using a controlled experiment with 13,500 observations across three LLMs (GPT-4.1 Mini, GPT-5 Mini, Kimi K2-0905), the research tested hedonic versus utilitarian products under four persuasion conditions based on Cialdini’s principles. Results reveal differential persuasion sensitivity by product type: social proof increased the rate at which LLMs expressed high recommendation certainty for concert tickets from 9.6% to 65.6%, while authority appeals reduced certainty for utilitarian products. This asymmetric pattern persisted across all models and partially mirrors human consumer psychology, suggesting LLMs internalized decision frameworks from training data. The study contributes to IS research by extending the hedonic-utilitarian framework to AI-mediated decision support and connecting LLM persuasion susceptibility to debates on technology trust. These findings have practical implications for how persuasive content shapes AI-mediated consumer decision support.

title: Evaluation of validity and reliability of AI Chatbots as public sources of information on dental trauma
authors: Johnson A.J.; Singh T.K.; Gupta A.; Sankar H.; Gill I.; Shalini M.; Mohan N.
abstract: Aim: This study aimed to assess the validity and reliability of AI chatbots, including Bing, ChatGPT 3.5, Google Gemini, and Claude AI, in addressing frequently asked questions (FAQs) related to dental trauma. Methodology: A set of 30 FAQs was initially formulated by collecting responses from four AI chatbots. A panel comprising expert endodontists and maxillofacial surgeons then refined these to a final selection of 20 questions. Each question was entered into each chatbot three times, generating a total of 240 responses. These responses were evaluated using the Global Quality Score (GQS) on a 5-point Likert scale (5: strongly agree; 4: agree; 3: neutral; 2: disagree; 1: strongly disagree). Any disagreements in scoring were resolved through evidence-based discussions. The validity of the responses was determined by categorizing them as valid or invalid based on two thresholds: a low threshold (scores of ≥ 4 for all three responses) and a high threshold (scores of 5 for all three responses). A chi-squared test was used to compare the validity of the responses between the chatbots. Cronbach's alpha was calculated to assess the reliability by evaluating the consistency of repeated responses from each chatbot. Conclusion: The results indicate that the Claude AI chatbot demonstrated superior validity and reliability compared to ChatGPT and Google Gemini, whereas Bing was found to be less reliable. These findings underscore the need for authorities to establish strict guidelines to ensure the accuracy of medical information provided by AI chatbots.

title: Psychotherapists’ Trust, Distrust, and Generative AI Practices in Psychotherapy: Qualitative Study
authors: Kuang J.; Pope A.L.; Zhang Y.
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in mental health care, from client-facing chatbots to clinician-facing documentation aids. Psychotherapists’ willingness to rely on—or withhold reliance from—these tools has significant implications for care quality, yet little is known about how practicing clinicians calibrate trust and distrust in GenAI across tasks and contexts. Given that the therapeutic relationship is central to psychotherapy outcomes, understanding how GenAI intersects with this relational foundation is essential for responsible integration. Objective: This study aims to examine (1) psychotherapists’ experiences with, perceptions of, and trust or distrust in GenAI in therapeutic contexts and (2) how they perceive the role of GenAI within the therapeutic relationship and how their perceptions shape their trust and distrust in GenAI. Methods: We conducted a qualitative interview study using semistructured interviews with 18 actively practicing psychotherapists in the United States between January and May 2025. Participants were recruited through professional mailing lists, social media, and snowball sampling. Interviews (≈60 min each) were conducted via Zoom and explored psychotherapists’ experiences with, perceptions of, and trust or distrust in GenAI in therapeutic contexts. Data were analyzed using the general inductive approach, with iterative coding and team-based interpretation to identify themes. Results: Our findings show that psychotherapists’ GenAI adoption was highly individualized and contingent on maintaining professional role integrity—not merely technical oversight. Trust was sustained when GenAI operated in clinician-supervised, supportive roles for low-stakes tasks (eg, documentation and brainstorming), but diminished when control shifted, tasks involved high-stakes clinical judgment, or GenAI threatened to encroach on the authentic human connection central to therapy. Participants articulated conditions for trust that went beyond “human-in-the-loop” monitoring to include preservation of interpretive authority, ethical responsibility, and relational primacy. Distrust also extended to the broader sociotechnical ecosystem, including concerns about commercial incentives, insurance pressures, and the absence of clear organizational guidelines. Conclusions: Psychotherapists’ perspectives offer critical insights into GenAI’s current usages in their professional practices and the conditions under which they are willing to trust and distrust GenAI tools. Their experiences highlight the importance of maintaining clinician control, ensuring contextual appropriateness, and preserving the human connection central to psychotherapy. Future work should further examine how therapeutic orientation, professional experience, and client characteristics shape trust and distrust in GenAI. As GenAI becomes more embedded in mental health care, research is also needed to explore how specific GenAI system features can be responsibly designed to support clinical workflows and enhance therapeutic relationships. Organizational and policy frameworks will be essential to ensure responsible, ethically aligned, and human-centered GenAI deployment in psychotherapy.

title: Framing the future of search: A discourse analysis of Google’s AI Overviews
authors: Weinbrand S.; Nagappa A.; Angus D.
abstract: This study investigates how Google’s AI Overviews (AIOs) – a major shift in the search engine landscape – are discursively framed by three key actors: Google, tech journalists, and Search Engine Optimisation (SEO) marketers. Drawing on platform studies and discourse theory, we combine Leximancer concept mapping with Critical Discourse Analysis to examine how these stakeholders construct, legitimise, and contest the meaning of AIOs across a broad corpus of grey literature, media coverage, and corporate blogs. Our findings reveal four dominant thematic frames: Generative AI Technologies and AI-Platform Wars, Reconfiguring Search: Let Google Do the Searching for You, Commercial Implications of AIOs, and AI Overviews – Utopia versus Dystopia. While Google frames AIOs as seamless innovations that enhance the user experience, journalists highlight issues of misinformation and epistemic opacity, and SEO marketers focus on the economic and strategic disruptions to visibility and discoverability. Crucially, our analysis underscores the absence of the user’s voice and a lack of attention to democratic, societal and environmental implications of AI-generated summaries. By analysing the discourse surrounding AIOs, this paper demonstrates that AIOs are not merely a new feature, but rather part of a broader shift in platform power and control over online knowledge. We argue that AIOs represent a key moment in the transformation of search, reshaping how trust, authority, and visibility are defined and challenged in the age of AI.

title: Diabetes Prediction with Code-Based Mecical Insurance Claims Based on Multimodal Representations and Vision-Language Models
authors: Yang W.; Yoshimoto H.; Mitsutake N.; Goda K.
abstract: Chronic diseases associated with lifestyles, such as diabetes and hyperlipidemia, are growing in many countries. That leads to increased social security expenditures and insufficient medical resources. The optimization of data-driven medical systems is crucial for medical facilities and governments to make accurate medical planning and provide their citizens with quality medical services. A solution should be future demand prediction, allowing the authorities to understand the care demand that might be onset and to secure necessary medical resources in advance. This work aims to enable the prediction of future demands from public medical insurance claims (MICs). Japan has implemented a universal medical care insurance system in which citizens can receive necessary medical care. Public medical insurance covers the majority of medical services that insurance systems provide to citizens, and the medical insurance claims dataset potentially enables population-scale prediction. In particular, this work attempts to exploit large language models (LLMs) to realize the future demand prediction from medical insurance claims. However, medical insurance claims are semi-structured and recorded with specific codes. The naïve use of LLMs offers poor prediction accuracy. To this end, we propose a multimodal representation for code-based MICs and a vision-language model for predicting medical demand. The experiments confirmed that our model achieved a significant improvement of 3.8 points in accuracy compared to the baseline system on diabetes cases.

title: Human-AI Symbiosis in Essay Assessment: A Human-in-the-Loop Scoring Model for Engineering Education
authors: Budayawan K.; Ganefri; Anwar M.; Asmara D.; Agustiarmi W.; Kurniadi D.
abstract: Essay evaluation is significant in engineering education because it allows lecturers to evaluate students' conceptual comprehension, technical reasoning, argumentation, and ability to explain engineering problem-solving procedures. However, hand essay scoring is frequently time-consuming, cognitively demanding, and vulnerable to inconsistency, especially when grading criteria are not explicitly operationalised. Recent developments in automated essay scoring, huge language models, and generative AI have created prospects to help assessment; yet, entirely automated scoring may reduce transparency, ignore contextual judgement, and undermine lecturer authority in assessment decision-making. This work presents a conceptual and technically defined human-in-the-loop scoring model for AI-assisted essay assessment in engineering education. The model incorporates analytic rubrics, rubric-guided prompting, retrieval-based knowledge sources, AI-assisted preliminary scoring, scoring rationales, feedback generation, lecturer validation, and revision-aware final scoring. To provide operational clarity, the study defines the AI-assisted scoring pipeline in terms of structured inputs, retrieval-supported context, prompt components, output schema, uncertainty flagging, lecturer validation, and an audit trail. The study also describes a preliminary pilot evaluation that included anonymised essay replies from 30 students who answered four essay questions, yielding 120 essay-response units and 480 dimension-level scoring judgements. The evaluation compares GPT-4o-mini-generated preliminary results to lecturer-approved scores using precise agreement, adjacent agreement, mean absolute error, Cohen's Kappa, and Quadratic Weighted Kappa. In the suggested workflow, AI serves as a decision-support component, producing preliminary scores, rationales, feedback suggestions, and noted issues, while lecturers review, revise, and make final assessment decisions. The model is expected to support more transparent, consistent, and formative essay assessment while maintaining lecturer authority and human responsibility in educational assessment.

title: Construction of Financial Risk Assessment Model Based on Text Mining and LLM Architecture
authors: Li Z.; Sui M.; Yang C.; Liu S.; Guan B.; Li X.
abstract: Faced with the challenges of accelerating growth in unstructured text data and increasing risk concealment in the financial market, this study constructs a financial risk assessment system that combines text mining with large language models (LLMs). This system forms an end-to-end architecture encompassing data, knowledge, models, services, and governance. The system collects multi source text, constructs a risk knowledge graph, and extracts key events and sentiment signals. These are then integrated into the LLM framework of retrieval augmented generation (RAG) and multi feature fusion to achieve credit risk prediction and default probability estimation. This experiment relies on the FinBen Lending Club dataset (2024) and conducts comparative experiments, ablation studies, error analysis, and stability tests. The model outperforms traditional structured models and plain text models in key evaluation indicators such as F1, MCC, and PR AUC. In scenarios of market environment changes, cross industry migration, and anti-interference, the model's stability and compliance performance are outstanding. This study designs an intelligent risk identification solution for financial institutions, which makes the identification process explainable, traceable, and auditable. This study has significant theoretical and practical impact on risk governance and decision support for banks, securities, insurance, and regulatory authorities.

title: Standards-Aligned Ethical Gating and Decision Telemetry for LLM-Assisted Mobile Robot Navigation: A Simulation Study
authors: Pandit P.K.; Singh A.; Galiya H.B.; Wu W.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly considered for autonomous robot decision support, but their non-deterministic outputs are difficult to validate in safety-critical settings. This paper presents a governance architecture for mobile robot navigation that incorporates LLM reasoning as a bounded advisory component without granting it direct control authority. The architecture combines schema-constrained LLM outputs, deterministic arbitration, a hard safety gate at the actuation interface, and structured telemetry for post-hoc audit. Implemented in ROS 2 Jazzy and evaluated in Gazebo Harmonic, the system is tested across four scenarios spanning obstacle avoidance, privacy-boundary enforcement, and an ethical dilemma requiring the robot to balance competing privacy and mission-urgency obligations. Over 2,400 simulation trials, the architecture achieved zero safety violations and zero decision instability. LLM participation ranged from 87% to 96% across scenarios, with deterministic fallback compensating where model confidence was lower. In the dilemma scenario, the system produced graduated responses with explicit tradeoff reasoning rather than binary outcomes. The results demonstrate that deterministic enforcement combined with structured telemetry can provide both runtime safety and auditable evidence for responsible deployment of LLM-Assisted autonomous systems.

title: The shift in ethical governance from traditional philosophy to algorithmic decision making
authors: de Marcellis-Warin N.; Melchior C.; Warin T.
abstract: This article examines how large language models (LLMs) act as a new kind of ethical authority by refusing to produce certain content. Using one model (LLaMA 3.2) and one task, paraphrasing about 100,000 tweets, we study the refusals the model issues and ask what norms they enforce and how consistently. A thematic analysis of a random sample of approximately 1000 refusals, with category frequencies estimated for the full dataset, shows that they concentrate in two norm families: misinformation, reflecting a concern for truth, and hateful or harmful speech, reflecting a concern for harm. The model applies these standards selectively, on the basis of the content rather than the user, and uniformly across very different topics and contexts. We interpret this uniform, non-adaptive enforcement, with appropriate caution, as a possible driver of value homogenization, while noting that our data measure the model’s behavior rather than its effects on society. We place these findings in a brief historical context, in which ethical authority has moved from philosophers and religious institutions to states and now to AI systems, and we weigh the benefits, a higher floor for online discourse, against the risks, the global imposition of a single, largely Western-derived standard by a small number of private firms. The study contributes a social-science reading of AI refusals as empirical evidence of the ethical boundaries these systems enforce.

title: Generative AI for enhanced risk management in SMEs
authors: Leonard E.; Sheehan B.; Mullins M.; Shannon D.
abstract: Establishing and sustaining small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) presents considerable challenges. Entrepreneurs must navigate limited resources and significant knowledge gaps across a spectrum of information requirements–from health and safety to corporate governance, taxation, and personnel management. Despite the extensive deployment of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) across sectors such as medicine, education, and finance, its application and research in SME risk management remain notably sparse. This research aims to bridge this gap by showcasing the benefits of GAI within the risk management cycle, which is critical to enhancing the prospects of success among smaller business entities. With rapid technological advancements and the widespread integration of GAI in office and home settings, an opportunity arises to develop customised risk management tools specifically tailored for SMEs. The analysis outlines a conceptual case study in the food and beverage sector, where an entrepreneur launches a new restaurant. The study tracks GAI’s iterative application across all phases of the risk management cycle: identification, comprehension, assessment, treatment, and monitoring. Specifically, it integrates retrieval augmented generation (RAG), which accesses and incorporates information from the Irish Health and Safety Authority (HSA) into its processes. Additionally, GAI assistants are created and employed to execute tasks integral to the risk management cycle, such as calculating risk factors. A key outcome is the creation of a risk register for each potential hazard, demonstrating GAI’s practical application in risk assessment. These tools illustrate the potential of GAI to navigate the complex, information-dense, and regulatory-heavy landscape of contemporary business environments. This exploration underscores how GAI can improve decision-making and risk evaluation and promotes further discussion and research on developing user-friendly GAI technologies.

title: ‘Chattable’ Avatars: Using LLMs to Power Visitor Engagement with Historical Persons
authors: Jiang Z.; Qin Y.; Finnegan D.J.
abstract: Cultural Heritage institutions such as Galleries, Libraries, Archives, and Museums are tasked with preserving our history and heritage for future generations while engaging new audiences with an appetite for said engagement to be increasingly digital and interactive. To explore how advances in natural language processing, particularly large language models (LLMs), may help GLAMs in their mission, we designed a prototype ‘Chattable’ avatar, a 3D high-polygon animated character which visitors can talk to and interact with. We report the design of our avatar, and a workshop we conducted with curators and staff from a GLAM institution, to understand the problems, requirements, and opportunities LLMs present in the cultural heritage space. We present results from a qualitative analysis of our workshop highlighting themes such as trust, authority, social experience, and location, finding LLMs may be more suited to deployments focused on non-factual data dissemination. We conclude with implications for GLAMs and suggestions for future research to realise how best to integrate GenerativeAI like LLMs into the GLAM space.

title: Debiasing and Explainability Effectiveness of LLM Tuning: A Quantitative Approach
authors: Mauri L.; Preda F.; Damiani E.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often perpetuate implicit biases from user prompts, necessitating fine-tuning to enhance fairness and explainability. However, quantifying tuning efficacy remains an open problem. This paper introduces a novel Shapley value-based framework to evaluate the debiasing impact by analyzing token attributions in prompts. We propose a dual metric - Shapley Bias Distribution (SBD, using the Gini coefficient) and Shapley Bias Entropy (SBE) - to measure the concentration of contributions, distinguishing between single-term and multiple-term biases. To streamline the analysis, we further propose the Focused SHAP Entropy Ratio (FSER), a composite metric that integrates Gini-like inequality and entropy-like uncertainty via core-periphery decomposition, with an automated threshold for unbiased, task-adaptive assessment. Our experiments on a Corpus of Linguistic Acceptability (CoLA)-inspired benchmark demonstrate lower variance and decreased entropy post-tuning, signaling a sharper focus on salient tokens and improved bias isolation. Our metrics enable rigorous verification of tuning outcomes, revealing incomplete debiasing through persistent high entropy. This provides certification authorities with a palette of tools that enhance trustworthiness and facilitate scalable certification.

title: ESG insight: a structured data extraction and evaluation framework via LLM
authors: Zhou Y.; Wu X.; Xu X.; Xu W.
abstract: ESG Insight is an innovative framework designed for the automated extraction and analysis of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) data from corporate disclosures, addressing the demand for accurate and standardized ESG information retrieval. Integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) with Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), the framework comprises an ESG metadata module, a report preprocessing unit, a Multi-Agent system, and a Multimodal Processing component. Its performance was evaluated on a sample of 300 SSE-listed companies’ ESG reports from year 2023 and 2024 across nine industries. Utilizing DeepSeek, ESG Insight achieved 78.2% accuracy in quantitative data extraction and 85.1% in disclosure identification, significantly surpassing baseline models. The analysis revealed disclosure rates of 67.8% for environmental, 55.9% for social, and 72.3% for governance indicators, underscoring persistent transparency gaps, particularly in social metrics. Limitations include challenges in processing visual data, such as charts, with planned enhancements to the Multimodal Processing module. Future research should focus on developing industry-specific datasets and extending the framework’s application to policy documents. ESG Insight enhances ESG data analysis, enabling stakeholders, securities firms and regulatory authorities to evaluate corporate sustainability, promote transparency, and advance China’s sustainable development objectives in alignment with SSE guidelines.

title: Discussion Paper: Exploiting LLMs for Scam Automation: A Looming Threat
authors: Gressel G.; Pankajakshan R.; Mirsky Y.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled powerful new AI capabilities, but their potential misuse for automating scams and fraud poses a serious emerging threat. In this paper, we investigate how LLMs combined with speech synthesis and speech recognition could be leveraged to build automated systems for executing phone scams at scale. Our research reveals that current publicly accessible language models can, through advanced prompt engineering, mimic authorities and seek personal financial information, bypassing existing safeguards. As these models become more widely available, they significantly lower the barriers for executing complex AI-driven scams, including potential future threats like voice cloning for virtual kidnapping. Existing defences, such as passive detection is not suitable for synthetic voice over compressed channels. Therefore, we urgently call for multi-disciplinary research into user education, media forensics, regulatory measures, and AI safety enhancements to combat this growing risk. Without proactive measures, the rise in AI-enabled fraud could undermine consumer trust in the digital and economic landscape, emphasizing the need for a comprehensive strategy to prevent automated fraud.

title: A Novel Notice to Airmen Description Generator Framework Based on String Matching Retrieval Augmented Generation
authors: Alfatih M.I.; Adhi Wibowo S.; Wisesty U.N.; Aulia I.; Zulmi M.A.; Irmadi Prasetyo R.; Catur K.A.; Hermawan J.; Azmi U.; Hasfrian R.N.
abstract: NOTAM (Notice to Airmen) is a vital component of the aviation industry, serving as a primary means of delivering a wide range of information to all parties involved in global flight operations. To ensure that this information is accessible and understandable, NOTAMs are written in accordance with regulations established by international aviation authorities. The demand for concise, clear, and universally applicable information means that NOTAMs employ a complex set of rules, abbreviations, and codifications. In this study, we developed a framework that enables the generation of NOTAM descriptions from free-form natural language, making the process more intuitive and accessible. Our results show that integrating our framework significantly improves accuracy when compared to using large language models (LLMs) without it. In our experiments with paired free-form text and NOTAM datasets, the framework achieved a top accuracy of 53.61%, which is 37.35% higher than results obtained without the framework. These findings highlight that LLMs alone lack the specialized knowledge necessary to generate proper NOTAM descriptions from free-form inputs. We believe this study offers valuable insights into the application of AI in the aviation sector and represents an important first step toward the development of comprehensive NOTAM generation systems.

title: Artificial Sages: Can a Language Model be an Epistemic Expert?
authors: Massaguer Gomez G.; Gaitan Torres A.; Garzon-Vico A.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLM) are being used, among other ends, to epistemically enquire and gain knowledge about different areas of investigation. In this paper, we will reflect on the nature of LLMs outputs and the epistemic status of the beliefs we can form from relying on them, paying special attention to their role in organizational contexts. The main thesis is that LLMs statements are and could increasingly be regarded by their users as a kind of objective expert testimony, with the epistemic authority that this entails. Although LLMs do not satisfy the criteria to be qualified as epistemic experts, due to, for example, their lack of intentionality, they still can be perceived as experts because of several reasons: our tendency to anthropomorphize, their appearance as objective, value-neutral and accurate entities, and the increasing distrust in human testimony. The search for information through LLMs instead of human epistemic experts, which could become more common with time within organizations and firms, raises several ethical issues, precisely because they are not experts in the strong sense. In this paper, we will investigate some ethical issues that arise from overreliance in LLMs, especially through the case of hallucinations.

title: FAIRTIQ in CEE: Leveraging Mobile Ticketing, Data Analytics, and AI for Smarter Public Transport in Data-Scarce Environments
authors: Belaieff A.; Ekes A.
abstract: FAIRTIQ is a pioneering Mobile Pay As You Go solution transforming public transport systems across Europe, with growing adoption in Central and Eastern Europe (CEE). Developed over eight years, FAIRTIQ has processed more than 366 million trips (as of March 2026) and remains the only MPAYG provider with seamless nationwide deployments in Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Austria, and Denmark. While designed as a simple, user-friendly app, FAIRTIQ functions as a powerful digital infrastructure for transport authorities and operators—especially valuable in the data-scarce CEE context. Its Insights Tool Family provides granular data on origin-destination flows, transfers, station loading, and person-kilometres, supporting evidence-based planning, performance evaluation, and revenue sharing. At the core of FAIRTIQ is a layered AI framework. Machine learning models detect modes of transport, recognise transfers, and classify passenger behaviours. Smart Stop, FAIRTIQ’s end-of-trip detection system, relies on environmental and behavioural signals to ensure accurate trip closure and billing. AI-based fraud detection flags suspicious patterns, such as late check-ins or trip manipulation, in real time. In customer service, FAIRTIQ employs generative AI to assist agents with contextual responses, while automated back-office tools handle routine corrections and refunds—enhancing operational efficiency and improving user satisfaction across the system.

title: Mitigating Cost Overruns in Public Works Procurement: Design Objectives for GenAI-Based Assistant Systems
authors: Pauken C.; Hartmann M.; Wimmer M.A.
abstract: Cost overruns remain a persistent challenge in public works procurement. Although extensive research has already examined potential causes and mitigation strategies, only modest improvements have been achieved thus far. Concurrently, Generative AI (GenAI) has been discussed as a key technology for digital transformation, with scholars anticipating GenAI to reduce workloads and costs, increase process efficiency, and strengthen quality control mechanisms. Hence, in this study, we explore how GenAI-based assistant systems can be designed to help experts in mitigating cost overruns in the domain of public works procurement. By applying Echeloned Design Science Research (eDSR), we combine findings from a systematic literature review with insights from on-site project workshops in a large federal state construction authority in Germany. We derive six validated design objectives that aim to strengthen quality assurance mechanisms during early procurement planning stages. Our findings suggest that GenAI-based systems can mitigate cost overruns in public works procurement by enabling change order risk predictions, legal compliance checks, document coherency checks, bidder question simulations, multi-level quality assessments and semantic standardization of free text into standardized items. Anticipated implementation constraints include a lack of AI-ready data, poor procurement document management, and high levels of change resistance within the organization.

title: A multilayered analysis of university students’ experiences with human and AI-based feedback: A comparative examination of BERTopic, LLM models, and mixture of agents approaches
authors: Yildiz Durak H.; Onan A.
abstract: This study presents a multilayered text analysis framework for examining university students’ experiences with human- and artificial intelligence (AI)-based feedback. The empirical corpus consisted of 322 feedback-related reflection statements obtained from 110 undergraduate students. The analysis combined data preprocessing, corpus-driven thematic modeling with BERTopic, zero-shot thematic extraction using large language models (LLMs), ensemble-based semantic alignment, psycholinguistic emotion–theme integration, and high-resolution thematic refinement through a Mixture of Agents (MoA) framework. BERTopic identified six core themes: trust and transparency, cognitive load and clarity, learning contribution and perceived benefit, emotional discomfort and uncertainty, human-AI comparison, and complementary feedback expectations. The results showed that students’ feedback experiences were multidimensional, involving cognitive, affective, explanatory, and comparative dimensions rather than a simple preference for either feedback source. BERTopic provided a stable corpus-grounded thematic baseline, whereas Large Language Model (LLM)-based zero-shot extraction produced pedagogically interpretable and conceptually expressive theme labels. The ensemble approach reduced variation across individual LLM outputs by consolidating semantically similar labels. MoA further refined thematic distinctions and improved emotion–topic alignment, particularly in statements involving cognitive ambiguity or emotionally charged feedback experiences. Comparative analyses indicated that AI-based feedback was more strongly associated with speed, accessibility, consistency, and immediate learning support, whereas human feedback was more strongly associated with contextual richness, empathy, pedagogical explanation, and perceived authority. The findings suggest that effective feedback design should combine the scalability and immediacy of AI-based feedback with human oversight, contextual interpretation, emotional calibration, and transparent justification. Overall, the study contributes to learning analytics and feedback research by demonstrating how corpus-driven topic modeling, LLM-based interpretation, ensemble alignment, and MoA-based refinement can be integrated to model the cognitive and affective dimensions of students’ feedback experiences.

title: Unmasking the Fake: Designing Explainable AI Agents for Autonomous Deepfake Mitigation
authors: Kumar P.S.; Ramanamurthy P.V.; Teja P.B.; Prasad M.S.L.; Mishra S.; Sunny G.S.
abstract: The fast progress of generative AI technologies has enabled the widespread generation and sharing of manipulated media, called deep fakes. These synthetic video and audio could ultimately undermine digital trust, privacy, and public safety. Many traditional systems for detecting deepfakes are black-box systems, providing limited transparency, interpretability, and real-world usability. The systems can be very limited in terms of explain ability and autonomous response, making it challenging for users, institutions, and authorities to validate authenticity, with timeliness, if needed.This paper introduces an Explainable AI-based Autonomous Deepfake Detection System that detects, interprets, and reasons about deepfake content in media files. The proposed system leverages MTCNN for face detection and InceptionResNetV1 for detecting deepfakes, using facial embeddings as classifiers. This system uses Gemini AI APIs, in two ways, as a modality to produce multimodal explanations for the detected outputs and uses Gemini's verification of evidence function through Google Search. The proposed architecture is also designed to analyze audio deepfakes, to detect manipulated voices and lip-sync mismatches, and to incorporate recommendations about evidence verification of manipulated content. Upon discovering possible deepfakes, the AI agent performs contextual actions on its own-providing human-readable explanations, searching for original content online, and documenting metadata and timestamps for compliance.

title: ‘Whack the prompt in there and see what it says’: making sense of Communicative AI in education
authors: Perrotta C.; Eedelouei S.
abstract: Using a communication lens, this article shows how interactions with a persuasive, but not entirely trustworthy, artificial partner (ChatGPT) are explained and ‘made sense of’ in an educational setting. The argument draws on a year-long qualitative study in a language school for international students. The findings draw attention to communicative negotiations about contextual criteria of authority, pedagogical meaning, and trust. In particular, the fieldwork highlighted three distinct dynamics: (a) retrospective rationalisations of AI use and misuse shaping teachers’ sensemaking; (b) simple forms of tactical prompting to accomplish basic tasks among students and (c) a moment-to-moment interplay of communicative roles, accompanied by situational variations in trust attribution. These findings suggest that a focus on pragmatic communicative interactions is a productive avenue of empirical research in education technology research. In the conclusion, the article reflects on the possibility that the analysis of projections, expectations, and desires flowing from human agents to communicative AI systems–and vice versa–could encourage the creation of educational practices of human distinctiveness.

title: From Sound to Risk: Streaming Audio Flags for Real-World Hazard Inference Based on AI
authors: Potamitis I.
abstract: Seconds count differently for people in danger. We present a real-time streaming pipeline for audio-based detection of hazardous life events affecting life and property. The system operates online rather than as a retrospective analysis tool. Its objective is to reduce the latency between the occurrence of a crime, conflict, or accident and the corresponding response by authorities. The key idea is to map reality as perceived by audio into a written story and question the text via a large language model. The method integrates streaming, zero-shot algorithms in an online decoding mode that convert sound into short, interpretable tokens, which are processed by a lightweight language model. CLAP text–audio prompting identifies agitation, panic, and distress cues, combined with conversational dynamics derived from speaker diarization. Lexical information is obtained through streaming automatic speech recognition, while general audio events are detected by a streaming version of Audio Spectrogram Transformer tagger. Prosodic features are incorporated using pitch- and energy-based rules derived from robust F0 tracking and periodicity measures. The system uses a large language model configured for online decoding and outputs binary (YES/NO) life-threatening risk decisions every two seconds, along with a brief justification and a final session-level verdict. The system emphasizes interpretability and accountability. We evaluate it on a subset of the X-Violence dataset, comprising only real-world videos. We release code, prompts, decision policies, evaluation splits, and example logs to enable the community to replicate, critique, and extend our blueprint.

title: Ontology-Driven Legal Rule Auditor for Secure, Trustworthy, and Governed RAG Systems
authors: Akremi A.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have significant potential in regulated domains such as law, healthcare, and compliance, where users need help interpreting complex rules and documents. However, these domains also make the risks of Large Language Models especially serious: a system may hallucinate legal authority, rely on outdated rules, mix jurisdictions, or expose sensitive information. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) reduces these risks by grounding the model’s answer in a curated document corpus, but standard RAG still does not guarantee that the retrieved sources are legally valid, up to date, applicable to the correct jurisdiction, or safe to use. In this paper, we present an ontology-governed approach to legal RAG. The central idea is to use a legal ontology not merely as background knowledge, but as an active control layer. Before retrieval, the ontology filters legal sources by jurisdiction, topic, lifecycle status, and temporal validity. After generation, validation rules check whether the answer is supported by approved evidence, cites valid legal sources, respects jurisdictional boundaries, and avoids unsafe or privacy-violating content. The system also records retrieval, validation, and response-generation steps in an audit trail to support later review. In this way, the proposed Legal Rule Auditor extends Graph RAG from a retrieval-enhancement technique into a governance architecture for legal question answering. Its goal is not simply to improve answer relevance, but to ensure that answers are legally grounded, trusted, current, jurisdictionally appropriate, and traceable.

title: Trustworthy Digital Auxiliary Processes for Sustainable Energy Utilization: A Targeted Process-Oriented Review and Conceptual Evidence-to-Review Framework
authors: Moon J.
abstract: Sustainable energy systems increasingly rely on digital auxiliary processes that convert telemetry, forecasts, diagnostic evidence, and operating rules into reviewable information for authorized human decision-makers. This targeted review develops a transparent and traceable conceptual evidence-to-review framework for photovoltaic, wind, storage, fuel-cell, and converter-coupled systems. The coded review pool comprised 100 sources, including 75 analytical and 25 contextual sources; 10 additional references supported methodological, technical, and case-specific context and were not included in thematic coding. A six-stage thematic analysis, supported by a revision-stage coding audit, identified five analytical layers: data-quality control, forecasting and uncertainty, explanation diagnostics, constrained evidence briefing, and accountable human review. These layers were translated into an eight-stage advisory architecture that separates evidence preparation, validation, briefing, and review from the authorized control plane. No direct large-language-model-to-controller or model-to-asset path is permitted. An illustrative Jeju scenario traces one evidence record through the architecture and shows how safety conditions, evidence admissibility, and procedural authority lead to CHECK, HOLD, or ESCALATE outcomes. The review concludes that trustworthy digital support requires traceable evidence, deterministic safety and rule boundaries, and accountable human authorization.

title: AI Calibracy: A Future-Ready Competency Framework in AI-Supported Professional Judgment and Decision Making
authors: Sepasgozar S.M.E.
abstract: AI Calibracy is a developmental competency that is defined in this entry as a learner’s or practitioner’s capacity to examine, coordinate, and progressively improve their judgment, external fresh evidence, computational models or simulations, and artificial intelligence (AI) within a specific decision context. What can be progressively improved is categorized into four bases of reliance, named as SEMA: Self, Evidence, Model or Simulation, and AI, and discussed in the paper. AI Calibracy is not supposed to prescribe a fixed hierarchy, numerical weighting, or a universal division of authority among these contributors. Instead, it identifies the capabilities required to recognize their relevance, limitations, assumptions, disagreements, and implications for professional judgment. The competency is introduced and also developed through the reliance calibration and regulation cycle (RCRC), as a process in which learners form an initial judgment, inspect evidence, test models, interrogate AI outputs, compare findings, identify uncertainty, revise their judgment and confidence, and reflect on outcomes across repeated tasks. In this concept, AI includes not only generative AI but also various functions such as predictive, diagnostic, recommendation, optimization, computer-vision, decision-support, and autonomous or semi-autonomous systems. AI Calibracy provides a definition for leadership, educators, curriculum design, pedagogy, professional development, assessment, and research into the capabilities required for responsible, as task-specific warrant and context-sensitive practice in AI-enabled environments.

title: AI and higher education: teachers' perceptions of students' ethical tensions in online pedagogical methods
authors: Baoyi W.; Khan F.U.
abstract: The emergence and development of generative AI tools have benefited higher education but have also created several ethical tensions in the educational system. This tension is higher in online teaching environments, where students often rely on AI tools. Previous studies have addressed ethical issues, yet how these issues have emerged across various teaching methods in online AI-driven classes has been overlooked. To address this gap, this qualitative study investigates teachers' perceptions about their students' ethical issues across five pedagogical methodologies: direct method, content and language integrating learning, task-based language teaching, communicative language teaching, and community language learning. These five methods represent widely used approaches to second- or foreign-language teaching rather than instructional methods in general, and the findings are accordingly specific to language-acquisition classrooms. Using thematic analysis of interviews with 25 teachers, this research recognized 20 unique ethical tensions across five teaching methodologies. These findings are synthesized into a holistic framework comprising three overarching ethical domains: authenticity of learning, authority challenge, and collaborative dynamics. Based on this framework, this research highlights the need for moving beyond general frameworks to method-based ethical policies in education. This research emphasizes a process-oriented assessment framework to ensure transparency in education and mitigate the risk of unethical issues and tensions in the educational system. Further implications for students, teachers, and policy makers have been discussed.

title: Rethinking teacher-student dynamics in an AI-enhanced mathematics classroom
authors: Canonigo A.M.
abstract: This study examines the evolving teacher-student dynamics in AI-enhanced mathematics classrooms, focusing on perception gaps regarding student independence, instructional clarity, and teacher authority. Using positioning theory as a framework, the findings reveal that while teachers assume AI promotes autonomy, students continue to require structured guidance. Significant discrepancies also emerge in instructional clarity, with teachers overestimating the intuitiveness of AI-enhanced learning environments. Furthermore, while educators believe they provide sufficient encouragement, students often do not perceive it, highlighting the need for more explicit support strategies. The study highlights the importance of structured scaffolding, clear instructional explanations, and balanced teacher authority when integrating AI tools like GeoGebra and ChatGPT. AI should serve as an enhancement to teacher instruction rather than a replacement, ensuring deep conceptual engagement rather than surface-level answer retrieval. Limitations include the study’s short-term scope, reliance on self-reported data, and focus on specific AI tools. Future research should investigate the long-term impact of AI-enhanced learning, comparative studies of different AI tools, and strategies for fostering responsible AI use. Addressing these areas will help bridge teacher-student perception gaps and optimize AI’s role in mathematics education, ensuring meaningful, student-centered learning experiences.

title: AI Significance in Higher Education: A Comparative Study Across the Polish Universities
authors: Soltysik-Piorunkiewicz A.; Chmielarz W.; Kossowska-Lai M.
abstract: The paper aims to show artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education based on a study in a Polish environment. In this study, the awareness of AI, particularly ChatGPT, was shown across Polish universities. This research was carried out in three selected universities: the University of Economics in Katowice (UE Kat), the University of Warsaw (UW), and the Jagiellonian University in Krakow (JU). Data were collected using a mixed method of PAPI (Paper and Pencil Interviewing) and CAPI (Computer Assisted Personal Interview). The surveys were distributed in a partially targeted manner in the academic environment to randomly selected groups of students. After that the collected data were processed: statistical indicators, distance measures, and tests were calculated. Thanks to the analysis of the results, it was possible to identify the level of artificial intelligence awareness in the studied environment and understand how respondents qualify for its usage. The originality of the research lies in the comprehensive treatment of the topic and its presentation in terms of gender and university location. The results may be useful to university authorities and researchers dealing with the applications of artificial intelligence in economic, and social life.

title: LLMs in the SOC: An Empirical Study of Human-AI Collaboration in Security Operations Centres
authors: Singh R.; Tariq S.; Jalalvand F.; Chhetri M.B.; Nepal S.; Paris C.; Lochner M.
abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into Security Operations Centres (SOCs) presents a transformative, yet still evolving, opportunity to reduce analyst workload through human-AI collaboration. However, their real-world application in SOCs remains underexplored. To address this gap, we present a longitudinal study of 3,090 analyst queries from 45 SOC analysts over 10 months. Our analysis reveals that analysts use LLMs as on-demand aids for sensemaking and context-building, rather than for making high-stakes determinations, preserving analyst decision authority. The majority of queries are related to interpreting low-level telemetry (e.g., commands) and refining technical communication through short (1-3 turn) interactions. Notably, 93 of queries align with established cybersecurity competencies (NICE Framework), underscoring the relevance of LLM use for SOC-related tasks. Despite variations in tasks and engagement, usage trends indicate a shift from occasional exploration to routine integration, with growing adoption and sustained use among a subset of analysts. We find that LLMs function as flexible, on-demand cognitive aids that augment, rather than replace, SOC expertise. Our study provides actionable guidance for designing context-aware, human-centred AI assistance in security operations, highlighting the need for further in-the-wild research on real-world analyst-LLM collaboration, challenges, and impacts.

title: KnowPath: An LLM-Supported Knowledge Graph Construction and Path Finding Framework to Explainable MOOC Recommendations
authors: Zhu J.; Chen Z.; Meo P.D.; Guan J.; Han Z.; Shi W.
abstract: The proliferation of Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) has created an urgent need for advanced course recommendation systems (RS). Course recommendations in MOOCs require transparent motivations to justify course selection, as there are often many courses with the same title, but which vary widely in content, duration, learning resources provided, and the academic authority of the instructor. Explainable recommendations are crucial to ensure that recommended courses fit well with learners’ needs and increase the chance of successful course completion, but unfortunately existing RS for MOOCs struggle to provide explainable recommendations. In this article, we present KnowPath, a novel RS for MOOCs, which generates effective and explainable recommendations. KnowPath uses open source Large Language Models (LLMs) to construct knowledge graphs (KGs) capable of accurately capturing complex relationships between MOOC entities (e.g., learners, instructors, educational resources) and employs Reinforcement Learning to align the output of an LLM with learner preferences. Extensive experiments on two public datasets (XueTang and COCO) demonstrate the superior performance and generalizability of KnowPath, underlining its potential to revolutionize the field of personalized online education.

title: Evaluating AI-assisted customer verification for synthetic nucleic acid screening
authors: Acelas A.; Palya H.; Flyangolts K.; Fady P.-E.; Nelson C.
abstract: Legitimacy screening, the process of verifying the identity and purpose of customers ordering synthetic nucleic acids, is a primary safeguard against the misuse of synthetic biology. However, the associated costs discourage the adoption of screening practices. To evaluate whether AI tools can facilitate this process, we tested five large language models on five verification tasks using customer profiles of life sciences researchers from around the world. We compared AI performance against an expert human baseline on flag accuracy, source quality, source fidelity, and cost. Flag accuracy of the best-performing model (Gemini 2.5 Pro with four bibliographic and sanctions APIs) was statistically indistinguishable from the human baseline at 90.2% and 89.0% (Formula presented). Gemini 2.5 Pro performed at or above the human baseline on source quality and fidelity, at roughly one-tenth of the cost ($1.18 vs. $14.04 per customer). For information-gathering tasks, which excluded the human review step, costs averaged $0.23 per customer, around 50 times cheaper than human screening. These results support piloting AI assistance at the information-gathering step of legitimacy screening at providers of synthetic nucleic acids and other dual-use biotechnology products, with human reviewers retaining authority over follow-up communication and order fulfillment decisions.

title: Hegemonikon and AI
authors: Koutsotasios C.A.; Vavouras E.
abstract: The central ethical problem raised by artificial intelligence is not whether AI systems can “reason” in a functional sense, but whether their use preserves a centre of judgment that can be held responsible. Beginning with large language models, it distinguishes linguistic fluency from scientific validity, ethical commitment, and accountability. Enter the Stoic concept of the hegemonikon-the capacity for assent that directs the mind-as a framework for understanding intellectual creation and decision-making. This framework is extended by analogy to institutions clarifying when AI supports human judgment and when it replaces decision-making authority. The argument is applied to various fields and leads to five principles for the ethical use of AI: disclosure, attribution, critical engagement with AI outputs, meaningful human oversight, and augmentation rather than replacement. Responsible AI governance requires institutions to preserve decision-making structures that are identifiable, open to challenge and revision, and subject to accountability.<sup>1</sup>.

title: Metadata-Driven RAG Architecture for Context-Aware University Information Retrieval
authors: Aberathna Y.M.B.D.; Asanka P.P.G.D.; Mahanama T.V.; Kariyapperuma J.
abstract: General-purpose Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently produce generic or hallucinated responses when addressing university-specific queries, as they lack personalization aligned with individual student contexts. This paper proposes an enhanced Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system that incorporates university ontology with rule-based metadata filtering to generate personalized and accurate responses tailored to students' academic profiles. The system integrates student metadata, such as batch, department, degree program, and academic year with institutional hierarchy modelling to filter and prioritize retrieved documents prior to response generation. The enhancement is driven by two core mechanisms: metadata-based filtering removes contextually irrelevant documents based on student profiles and document attributes, while ontology-driven prioritization ranks information sources according to institutional authority structures and temporal relevance. The system was evaluated using a diverse set of academic and non-academic queries from the University of Kelaniya, where it consistently outperformed the baseline RAG model across all evaluation metrics. Retrieval precision and recall showed notable improvements, answer generation quality increased substantially, and human assessments indicated significant gains in factual accuracy, relevance, and completeness, with lower hallucinations. Overall, the findings demonstrate that the integration of domain-specific ontological knowledge with metadata-driven filtering markedly improves RAG performance in educational settings, offering a scalable approach for context-aware academic support systems.

title: Do AIs have politics? Thinking about ChatGPT through the work of Langdon Winner
authors: Fernandez L.
abstract: Since at least the 1960s, scholars, pundits and the general public have been worried about AI hype – the tendency to project more power, agency and intelligence on AI than it really has. To counter this tendency, academics often warn against anthropomorphizing AI or assuming that its impacts on society are inevitable. While these are sensible cautions, taken too far, they risk ignoring the way the design of AI actually can shape and condition how power and authority is distributed in society – and in academia. How, then, to see AI? Is it merely a tool people use for their own ends? Or can it hijack these ends? This paper argues that Langdon Winner provides provocative frameworks for tackling these questions.

title: Emerging frontiers and challenges of artificial intelligence in PSMA-PET imaging: pioneering a new chapter in prostate cancer care
authors: Wang Y.; Cheng C.; Huang B.; Zuo C.
abstract: Prostate-specific membrane antigen positron emission tomography (PSMA-PET) has become pivotal in prostate cancer (PCa) management, offering superior sensitivity over conventional imaging for detecting tumors, metastases, and biochemical recurrence. However, interpretive subjectivity, workflow inefficiencies, and heterogeneous PSMA expression remain significant limitations. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly radiomics and deep learning, addresses these challenges by enabling automated lesion analysis and image enhancement. This review examines the impact of AI across the PSMA-PET workflow, covering optimized image acquisition (e.g., low-dose protocols, motion correction), enhanced interpretation (e.g., lesion characterization, prognostic stratification), and personalized theranostics (e.g., treatment response forecasting, radioligand therapy dosimetry). Despite promising multicenter validation, challenges remain in annotation standardization, data heterogeneity, model generalizability, interpretability, regulatory integration, and ethics. We further discuss emerging frontiers, including multimodal multi-omic integration, generative AI, and AI-driven clinical decision support systems. Notably, we highlight the evolving role of nuclear medicine physicians and radiologists as integrators of AI-derived biomarkers, who validate AI outputs for high-stakes decisions, retain interpretive authority for complex cases, and oversee quality assurance, ensuring that AI augments rather than replaces specialist expertise. These advances position AI-integrated PSMA-PET to drive precision oncology, with key pathways outlined for clinical translation and future innovation in PCa care.

title: Beyond efficiency: epistemic well-being at work under algorithmic governance
authors: Salazar-Altamirano M.A.; Ravina-Ripoll R.
abstract: Workplace well-being research has generated extensive evidence on subjective experience and on organisational antecedents, such as leadership, climate, justice, and work design. Yet, these conditions are usually theorised as predictors of affective, evaluative, or functioning outcomes rather than as constitutive arrangements that determine whether workers can exercise professional judgement with practical consequence. In parallel, debates on artificial intelligence (AI) often frame intelligent technologies as instruments of efficiency, optimisation, or control. Focusing on systems whose outputs enter consequential organisational evaluation and decision-making (including algorithmic management, predictive analytics, automated decision-making, decision-support systems, workplace surveillance, and generative AI) this article asks whether organisational arrangements preserve or erode the capacity for judgement, contestation, and epistemic responsibility. It introduces Epistemic Well-being at Work (EWW) as an organisational condition in which individuals and collectives can exercise responsible judgement within socio-technical structures of authority. Drawing on the view of intelligent technologies as emergent epistemic regimes, this paper develops the Human Sustainability and Epistemic Well-being Framework (HSEW-F), linking AI-mediated governance, human dignity at work, and sustainable organisational well-being. The contribution is conceptual: it extends, rather than displaces, established well-being approaches by making the effective exercise of epistemic agency visible as a structural condition of human sustainability.

title: Believing the Algorithm: AI and the Transformation of Popular Belief in India
authors: Roy M.; Basistha N.
abstract: AI technologies in India are not only transforming digital habits but also reshaping belief systems. From religious chatbots to political propaganda and tools like ChatGPT, AI now mediates truth, tradition, and trust. Drawing on sociological and media theories, this chapter explores AI as a cultural actor in India's media ecology. Based on a mixed- methods survey of 150-300 respondents and analysis of AI- mediated content, it shows how algorithms reinforce dominant narratives across caste, gender, and religion. Using concepts like habitus and mediatization, it examines how repeated AI use reshapes understandings of knowledge and authority. The chapter calls for culturally rooted AI policies and critical digital literacy, arguing that AI is emerging as an ideological force shaping belief in an automated society.

title: Readability, information quality, and safety of AI chatbot responses to common questions about ostomy care: A cross-sectional digital health evaluation
authors: Zhang Y.; Li X.; Su J.; Yuan L.I.; Zhou A.; Chen L.; Zhang H.
abstract: Background: Patients with ostomies often require timely, understandable, and reliable guidance for self-care after surgery. Although AI chatbots are increasingly used as accessible sources of health information, the quality and safety of their responses for ostomy care remain uncertain. Objective: To compare information quality, readability, and text-level safety across five chatbots answering common ostomy-care questions. Methods: We submitted forty-six matched patient-facing ostomy-care questions once to five chatbots (ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity AI, DeepSeek, and Doubao) through official web interfaces on March 31, 2026, yielding 230 first responses. Responses were assessed with DISCERN, EQIP, Global Quality Score (GQS), JAMA benchmarks, six readability indices, and a guideline-based audit. Citation review was limited to Perplexity AI, the only system displaying source links. Comparisons used Friedman, Wilcoxon, and Cochran’s Q tests with multiplicity adjustment. Results: Scores differed across all four measures of quality and all six readability indices after Holm correction (adjusted P<.001). Perplexity AI in Pro Search mode scored higher on DISCERN, EQIP, and JAMA. Of its 1,721 citations, 18.9% were nonacademic or low-authority and 5.3% clinically inappropriate. DeepSeek had lower reading-grade estimates, but no system met the sixth-grade benchmark. Agreement was good for quantitative scores (ICC [2,1] =0.758–0.791) and high for qualitative coding (κ=0.830–0.842). Guideline deviations and potential text-level safety risks occurred across systems, with no significant adjusted between-system differences. Conclusions: None was consistently suitable as a stand-alone source of ostomy education. Their responses may support patient education after professional review but should not replace clinician-guided instruction.

title: WHO OWNS ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE?
authors: Tully R.
abstract: This paper explores the complex landscape of AI-assisted and AI-generated work, examining the pressing concerns and issues regarding Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) and ownership in the future. AI presents unprecedented opportunities and challenges, potentially influencing every global citizen in profound ways. Against a backdrop of the historical evolution of disruptive technologies the paper navigates the current discourse and legal frameworks around AI and IPR. It underscores the pivotal role of authorship and ownership in shaping the intersection of AI and IP. The paper also considers the challenges faced by authorities grappling to regulate its application. Acknowledging the disruptive and contested nature of AI outputs in the context of IPR, the narrative raises ethical concerns around how AI is deployed and exploited. As AI becomes more ubiquitous, questions arise about its potential impact on the ecosystem which protects creative production and innovation, potentially posing a threat to established intellectual property norms. The paper considers the potential for a new AI/IP ecosystem as well as the intriguing possibility of AI itself being granted intellectual property rights, a development with far-reaching implications for global IP policy. The concluding focus underscores the profound implications of these issues on both Engineering and Design Practice and education, urging a careful consideration of how to harness the benefits of generative AI while preserving the integrity and motivation of human creative endeavours.

title: Applying artificial intelligence to cardiology: opportunities and risks
authors: Nicolosi G.L.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to change dramatically cardiology practice. Applying AI can allow integration of large language models with extremely large and complex cardiological data bases and cardiovascular imaging. In this way AI could help physicians and scientists in the diagnostic, prognostic and therapeutic approach to each individual patient, making real the possibility of a true precision cardiology. To reach this goal, there is a great need of a more collaborative, multidisciplinary and universalistic approach, avoiding any elite methodology leading to overfitting. Inclusion of structured and unstructured data sets could help the representation of the heterogeneity of the real world. Government Authorities, Scientific Societies and all other Institutional stakeholders, including patients, should be involved, with clear Institutional leadership, for the development of an Ethical Trustworthy AI, with shared rules and certification as Medical Devices.

title: Rehumanizing Intercultural Communication in AI-Supported Distance Language Education Through Empathy, Humor, and Ethical Awareness
authors: Gokce M.; Sen M.K.
abstract: The Rehumanizing Pedagogical Framework (RPF) advanced herein treats empathy, humor, and ethical awareness as assessable learning outcomes in AI-mediated intercultural communication within distance foreign language education. Grounded in intercultural communicative competence theory and human-machine communication research, the framework identifies four design mediators: task design, feedback design, interface affordances, and governance. These mediators preserve the relational core of intercultural learning while positioning AI as a pedagogical resource rather than an unchecked authority. The analysis situates these mediators within debates on agentic AI, culturalbias in large language models, and governance conditions that covary with perceived intercultural benefit. Evaluation triangulates self-reported dispositions, interactional evidence ofrepair and audience-safe humor, and ethical practice artifacts. The chapter concludes with a tiered research agenda and recommendations for programs seeking to integrate AI without eroding the human dimensions of intercultural dialogue.

title: Conversational Breakdown and Repair in Constraint-Heavy LLM-Based Architectures: A Trace-Based Taxonomy and Architectural Analysis for Reliable CUI Systems
authors: Perera K.J.P.G.; Nanayakkara S.S.; Huff E.W.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded in constraint-heavy conversational user interfaces that support state-changing tasks. While LLMs enable flexible dialogue, their probabilistic behavior introduces conversational breakdowns, including semantic misalignment, execution-state corruption, and pragmatic failure. Despite widespread deployment, limited systematic understanding exists of how such breakdowns manifest in correctness-critical domains or how architectural design influences recovery. We present a trace-based analysis of conversational breakdown and repair in LLM-based task-oriented agents using a controlled ordering domain with explicit state and policy enforcement. Dialogue traces were generated across three architectural variants: generative-controller, guardrailed-generative, and deterministic-controller. We derive a taxonomy of breakdown types and evaluate repair effectiveness using turn-based recovery delay and state restoration. Results show that breakdown patterns are architecture-sensitive. Beyond comparative evaluation, we present a reproducible trace-based methodology for stress-testing LLM-mediated conversational systems prior to deployment. These findings establish separation of generative interpretation from execution authority as a core principle for reliable conversational user interface engineering.

title: High-Stakes AI Chatbot Systems in Mental Health Care: A Systematic Literature Review from a Critical Safety Perspective
authors: Turk D.; Wu D.
abstract: AI chatbots and large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly used for mental health guidance, including by users in acute distress. In suicide, self-harm, and crisis contexts, incorrect or unsafe responses are safety critical because they can plausibly influence real-world help seeking, escalation, and harm. Using a PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta Analyses)-based systematic review, from a safety-critical perspective, this study aims to synthesize how high stake mental-health chatbot systems evaluate and handle suicide, self-harm, and crisis risks, what current evaluation practices and limitations are. We narratively synthesized nine selected peer reviewed full-text studies and cross-checked study-level coding using the PRISMA framework. Safety behaviors, decision authority/escalation structures, and failure modes were coded using "Yes/No/Unclear"and "Not assessed,", without inferring features absent from the papers. We found that evaluation methods were mostly heterogeneous and simulation based. Several latest studies directly stress that systems can produce unsafe or risky responses, and that crisis appropriate routing and monitoring are often missing or inconsistent, including specialist validated unsafe-answer findings and clinician comparison evidence of limited risk level sensitivity. Evaluation commonly relies on scripted testing rather than real-world monitoring, and escalation pathways are frequently absent, unspecified, or inconsistently described.

title: ALGORITHMIC ETHICS IN AI-CREATED ARTWORKS
authors: Dixit R.; Patil J.; Pujari K.A.; Puntambekar D.; Parmar Y.; Kaur G.
abstract: The information presented in this paper explores the changing ethical issues that come with AI-generated artworks, and how algorithms, datasets, and the behavior of model-layers, cultural sensitivity, and the governance structures influence artistic results. The research evaluates various aspects of ethical risk, such as the spread of bias, stylistic theft and misrepresentation of culture, as well as manipulation of identity. Based on a multi-layered analytical framework upheld by graphs, tables, and case studies, the study points out that the main ethical vulnerabilities are due to uneven datasets, obscure semantic-layer reasoning, and inadequate protection of culturally sensitive information. To illustrate how the failures of ethics are put into practice, the paper introduces five real-world case studies that include unauthorized style mimicry, distortion of Indigenous symbols, the bias of a demographic portrait, exploitation of community heritage datasets, and manipulation of identity by a deepfake to prove how they may fail in practice. The results show that governance interventions, including consent-driven datasets, fairness auditing, cultural-protection mechanisms, and identity safeguards, can greatly mitigate the harmful output, which is achieved through their regular use. The paper ends with an overview of the future directions that focus on contextual cultural intelligence, adaptive governance, semantic interpretability and community oriented data rights. The general aim is to influence the creation of morally accountable generative AI applications, which are cognizant of creative authority, culture, and social trust.
